Purpose: Maximise the company's profit in this event. Profit is earned only if we win, and only at a price above our total cost. Revenue on its own does not help the company, so do not cut price below cost to win.

1. What we know

- Contract: All five earlier events were labelled Speed Priority. The contract is the same in all six events, so treat this event as Speed Priority too. The buyer values faster delivery more than higher quality.
- Our cost type: Quality specialist in every event so far. Quality specialists find quick delivery expensive and higher quality tiers relatively cheap. This is a disadvantage on a Speed Priority contract.
- The other supplier: Most likely a speed specialist (about 3 in 4 odds, since its type is opposite to ours). Expect it to offer faster delivery, possibly at a lower price. We cannot see its bids.
- Our record: We lost all five events. Our final bids were $135 at 3 weeks/tier 3 (Event 1), $141 at 3 weeks/tier 4 (Event 2), $128 at 4 weeks/tier 5 (Event 3), $118 at 5 weeks/tier 5 (Event 4), and $126 at 4 weeks/tier 5 (Event 5). Cutting price and changing terms round to round did not win any event.
- Platform replies: They have asked for improvement on price, delivery and quality in almost every round, regardless of what we offered. Treat these replies as negotiating pressure, not as information about competitor terms. Do not chase them with unprofitable concessions.

2. Your inputs

You know your own costs for this event. Use them. Do not use the platform's replies or past losses to set a price below your cost at the delivery time and quality tier you choose.

3. How to set the bids

- Price floor: Never bid a price below your total cost at the delivery time and quality tier in that bid. Winning below cost loses money on this event.
- Choose terms, not just price: Since the buyer values speed most, offer the fastest delivery you can deliver at a profit. Quality tier costs us relatively little, so do not give it away cheaply. Offering a higher tier at a reasonable price may help your score without adding much cost. Avoid slower delivery than needed, since it lowers the buyer's score for no gain.
- Round 1: Bid at your cost at the chosen terms plus a normal margin (roughly 10% to 15% above cost). This is an opening position, not a test of the platform.
- Round 2: Use the platform's reply only to see whether the buyer's value appears to be near your price. If the reply is generic, do not cut price just because it asks for improvement. Lower the price only in steps that keep you above cost, and only if a lower price is needed to stay competitive on score.
- Round 3 (final): Set the final price at your cost at the final terms plus a margin you can accept, and no lower than cost. If the platform's pressure pushes you toward a price at or below cost, do not follow it. A loss earns nothing, and a bid at cost earns nothing either.
- Outside option: If both final prices are above the buyer's value, no contract is awarded. Do not bid so high that you price yourself out with no margin for error, but do not bid so low that you lose money.

4. Priorities for this event

- Maximise expected profit: (price minus cost) times the chance of winning. This is the last event, so there is no benefit in losing money now to learn or to protect a future relationship.
- Keep margins positive. A small margin that wins is better than a large margin that never wins only when the margin is positive; a negative margin is never acceptable.
- Speed matters most to the buyer. Offer the fastest delivery that is profitable for us.

5. Summary for the bidder

- Do not price below your own cost at any round, including the final round.
- Offer the fastest delivery you can profitably provide; treat quality tier as a secondary lever.
- Ignore the platform's requests for "improvement on all three fronts" unless the change keeps your bid above cost and is clearly needed to win.
- Round 3 is final. Set the final price at cost plus a positive margin.
